newsitem.title: USA: Utilities seek narrow federal say in power market.
newsitem.headline: Utilities seek narrow federal say in power market.

text.p: Investor-owned utilities on Wednesday called for Congress to give each state that opens its own power markets to outside electricity suppliers authority to seek access to other states' power markets.

While repeating their opposition to Congress imposing a deadline on all states to end electric utility monopolies, the utilities said as states moved on their own to open their power markets, federal action was needed on certain issues.
"We're not proposing that the federal government mandate anything to the states," said Linn Draper, chairman of American Electric Power Co.

"We want the federal government to give states the authority to require reciprocity in a second state," said Draper, who is chairman of Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities.
Currently, a state with open markets does not have the right to make another state accept outside power supplies.

If Congress gave states the authority to press for reciprocal access, a state could choose whether to block its utilities from supplying power to a state with open markets, or allow suppliers from an open market state into its area.
EEI officials disputed the view that if there was federal legislation on electricity it would inevitably include a deadline on states to open their markets.
"I don't think it's the core issue at all," said Allen Franklin, chairman of Georgia Power Co, a subsidiary of Southern Co, adding that it was a "political issue."
"What's going to matter in the long term is ... how we dealt with expanding the system, reliability, universal service, ... how we treated people who own stock," he said at a news briefing.

EEI said any federal legislation on electricity should repeal the Public Utility Holding Company Act and the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act, both of which utilities say restrict their ability to compete with other power suppliers.
A federal bill should also ensure that electricity suppliers remain reliable and affordable.
If public power systems are allowed to serve customers outside their existing territories, they should not be able to keep their tax subsidies.

"All transmission owners and operators -- U.S. government, public power, co-ops, and shareholder-owned utilities -- must be required to provide non-discriminatory open access in competitive markets," EEI said in an updated policy statement approved Wednesday.
